Walkout 2 Learn: Florida Students Walk Out of School to Protest DeSantis Education Policies
Florida students are taking their education into their own hands.
By
Rachel Janfaza
April 20, 2023
Zander Moricz
In lieu of taking a quintessential college spring-break trip, a group of youth organizers with
Walkout 2 Learn
went to Sarasota, Florida, for a weeklong brain dump before the group's upcoming day of action. From morning to night, the 12 youth activists sorted through data from Florida high schools, Instagram pages, and other social media accounts hoping to identify young Floridians eager to help their cause: a youth-led demonstration on Friday, April 21, to call out state lawmakers for their attacks on student rights.
Florida’s Republican-led state legislature and governor have passed multiple pieces of legislation that censor conversations in the classroom about gender, sexuality, and race, stripping rights from the very students the state’s schools are meant to serve.
“We cannot stop these hateful bills from becoming law,"
Zander Moricz
, the 19-year-old executive director and founder of Walkout 2 Learn, tells
Teen Vogue.
“They are ignoring us. They are not dealing with our perspectives.” So young people are pushing back with a day of walkouts and protests in response to Governor DeSantis’s agenda for students and schools, which includes the legislation dubbed the “Don’t Say Gay” law, the “Individual Freedom Act" (previously known as the “
Stop W.O.K.E. Act
"), attempts to ban AP African American studies in schools, and
efforts to pull funding for diversity programs at state colleges
. The Social Equity through Education Alliance (
SEE
) brought together a coalition of youth organizations from across the state and united a coalition of organizations on the ground in the lead up to Walkout 2 Learn.
Walkout 2 Learn organizer pickup at the Sarasota airport
Zander Moricz
Team dinner with Walkout 2 Learn organizers on day three in Sarasota
Zander Moricz
Walkout 2 Learn’s day of action is multipronged, but the heart of the event will be the school walkouts taking place at 12 p.m. on more than 300 Florida college and high school campuses, the coalition says.
In recognizing that young Floridians are feeling the brunt of these bills, Moricz says, the coalition behind Walkout 2 Learn is thinking “strategically” about how to provide “our communities with resources, networks, advocacy campaigns, activations.”
Beyond that, Moricz continues, “we're building power in the long term through registering young voters so that when we have a chance to regain that legislature, we're there to take it. When we have the chance to put good people in positions of power in Florida, we’re going to take it, while recognizing that we don't have time to spare. We need to provide ourselves with curriculum, with resources, with activations, with communities. It’s a short- and long-term strategy that allows survival and then, hopefully, a chance at reclaiming our state.”
At each walkout location, students will be prompted through a series of three steps in under 20 minutes, organizers say. First, students will walk out of their classrooms at more than 300 high school and college campuses across the state. Second, students will be asked to sign an ‘Active Pledge,’ which prompts folks to check their voter registration and to register to vote if they are unregistered. And third, they’ll hear a five-minute banned history lesson from a student peer.
All students will have the opportunity to sign up for a
virtual introductory-level African American studies course
, Walkout 2 Learn says. The group is working on creating the content for the course with African American studies professors from Historically Black Colleges and Universities and other colleges across the country.
Later on the planned day of action, at 6 p.m., there will be rallies in cities including Miami, Tallahassee, Jacksonville, and Orlando, featuring the likes of YouTuber and singer Gabi Demartino and elected officials such as Florida Rep. Anna Eskamani.
Walkout 2 Learn’s organizers also have personal reasons for getting involved. For instance, Maxx Fenning, now a 20-year-old senior at the University of Florida and part of the Walkout 2 Learn coalition, started an organization in high school called PRISM FL to “expand access to LGBTQ-inclusive education and sexual health resources in Florida.”
Though Fenning, who was the vice president and then president of his high school’s Gay Student Alliance (GSA), attended Palm Beach County public schools, which he says were “very affirming,” it wasn’t until his junior year of high school that he began to research LGBTQ+ history, learning about the
riots at the Stonewall Inn
, the difference between HIV and AIDS, and PrEP.
“I didn’t know all these things that are so, so impactful to queer people, and as the leader of an LGBTQ organization, that felt like a disservice,” he tells
Teen Vogue
, explaining why he started PRISM. Then, after the “Don’t Say Gay” bill started advancing through the legislature, which would go on to
restrict
how sexual orientation and gender identity are discussed in classrooms, Fenning says his “bubble popped.”
Organizers with Walkout 2 Learn in Sarasota, Florida at sunset after day four of work
Zander Moricz
“I realized that this gay mecca that I live in in South Florida doesn’t really dovetail with that Florida up in Tallahassee," he says. "And I realized just how much work needed to be done to create inclusive schools, to create inclusive curriculum where students really felt safe — and it has only gotten worse.”
Meanwhile, Gaby Diaz-Vendrell, a 20-year-old student at Barnard College who is from Jacksonville, says there was no official GSA at her religious high school and that her school’s sex-ed curriculum was very limited. “Our GSA operated on, like, underground patchworks, basically,” she tells
Teen Vogue
.
Given the way “resources were limited” for conversations about gender and sexuality while she was in high school, Diaz-Vendrell says, it’s concerning to see new bills pop up that will further limit students’ ability to have these types of dialogues.
One source of stress for Diaz-Vendrell’s friends is the bill to
ban public colleges and universities from using funds for diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives
. Diaz-Vendrell says she has friends at Florida state schools who are worried about the validity of their degrees and how their degrees will be perceived after they graduate, should certain classes be categorized under diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives.
“[I know] bio majors who [worry they] can’t get credit for bioethics because bioethics [can fall] under the umbrella of [diversity, equity, and inclusion] curriculum," she adds. "There are students who are terrified that the minute they graduate, they won't be able to get into grad school, they won't be able to get jobs, because the credibility of their degree will be diminished if this bill is legislated into law.”
Eighteen-year-old Cameron Driggers, who attends Flagler-Palm Coast High School — the same high school where gay activist
Jack Petocz
was suspended after distributing Pride flags during a rally against the “Don’t Say Gay” bill last year — says that while growing up in what he refers to as a “very conservative area” in Florida, he faced instances of discrimination because of his sexuality, such as when he tried to join athletic organizations.
Students at a 2022 Don't Say Gay walkout
Zander Moricz
“Fighting that and trying to seek accountability in a district that is very much controlled by this right-wing dogma and culture war that [stems] from Ron DeSantis’s governorship, I was unsuccessful,” Driggers says. “As an organizer, and especially in high school, I’ve done my best to try to bring students together to make their voice heard,” including helping organize a
book ban
protest and walkout against the “Don’t Say Gay” legislation.
“We need students organized,” Driggers says. “Organized people can be organized power. And I think Walkout 2 Learn is going to be a very transformative moment in doing just that.”
The organizers behind Walkout 2 Learn recognize that organizing can’t necessarily stop these “hateful and regressive bills from becoming law,” as Moricz puts it, but they aim to continue this fight with that in mind, rather than offering a “false promise” that Florida lawmakers can be persuaded to change course.
Says Moricz, “The more we organize around that false promise and the more we make people feel like they can stop these inevitable laws from coming into play, the more people give up, become fatigued and heartbroken, and feel like they failed."
While acknowledging  that these bills will likely become law, Walkout 2 Learn is adamant that it needs to reset expectations, noting that Florida’s young people are pragmatic about the state and their futures. (On April 19, the Florida Board of Education
approved DeSantis' request
to expand the “Don't Say Gay” law to all grades).
Walkout 2 Learn is also set on providing young people with a way to take matters into their own hands. If the Florida public school system will not educate its students, they will educate themselves. And they’ll register young voters along the way, so that this generation can elect new officials the next time around.
“It’s about eliminating political apathy, and that’s one of the biggest things that’s really affecting our youth today,” says Javier Gomez, an LGBTQ+ rights activist from Florida. “I think it’s super important that we finally realize that this [legislation] is affecting every one of us. It’s affecting queer people, it’s affecting the BIPOC community…. It’s going to affect you, one way or another.”
“Action is needed," Gomez continues. "And not in the ways we thought it was, but in the way that it is being worked on now. This is why we turn so many emotions into action…. We’re starting in Florida, but I see this going nationwide because there are so many anti-LGBTQ+ youth bills being passed everywhere.”
